title: Vesper and the Portrait
premise: Paloma Vasquez takes a teaching post at Marrow Creek School, where eleven students have vanished over decades and the town's records have been quietly rewritten to forget them. Her landlady's house holds a portrait of a woman named Vesper, and the mirrors begin lagging a second behind reality—showing, in that stolen second, what the house wants her to see. Paloma learns the missing children were taken by a song sung at dusk, a lullaby the town's founding families still hum to keep their own safe. To end it she must learn the song's final verse from Vesper's portrait without singing along, because joining the song means joining it forever; in the climax she teaches the verse back to the town's descendants as an accusation rather than a lullaby, breaking the pact at the cost of her own reflection.
about_author: Q. M. Ashgrove is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent nine years in small towns where the past was treated as negotiable. They write horror about institutions that protect themselves by forgetting, and they still keep meticulous notes.

chapters.title: Attendance
chapters.summary: Paloma arrives in Marrow Creek and notices her fifth-grade roster has more names than chairs, more names than memories. The principal deflects; the janitor warns her not to stay past dusk. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: uneasy curiosity masked by professional competence—she starts a documentation notebook on day one.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Hallway
chapters.summary: In her rented room, Paloma studies the portrait of Vesper Halloway, dated 1911, whose eyes seem repositioned each morning. A student, Dee, mentions a song the older kids sing at the fence line 'so the school lets you go home.' POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: the first cold drop of dread beneath routine.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: The mirrors begin reflecting the room a beat behind, and in that lag Paloma glimpses small hands pressed against glass from the inside. She cross-references old yearbooks and finds faces cut out with surgical care. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: rational denial cracking into methodical fear.

chapters.title: Dee's Verse
chapters.summary: Dee admits she knows two verses of the dusk song but refuses to sing the third, which 'isn't for kids.' That night a child's voice rehearses scales in Paloma's empty classroom. POV: alternating Paloma and Dee. Emotional beat: loyalty forming between teacher and student against a complicit town.

chapters.title: The Founders' Choir
chapters.summary: Paloma infiltrates a town archive night and discovers the founding families recorded the song as property—a covenant keeping their bloodline exempt while other children are 'collected.' The librarian burns her photocopies. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: righteous fury; justice outside the law becomes personal.

chapters.title: What the Portrait Knows
chapters.summary: Vesper begins appearing in the mirror-lag, mouthing words Paloma can't yet read: the third verse exists, and Vesper paid with her portrait-imprisonment for hiding it. Dee goes absent from school. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: grief sharpening into resolve—the price of survival made visible.

chapters.title: The Missing Class
chapters.summary: Following the lag-mirrors' clues, Paloma finds the school's sealed sub-basement: desks arranged in choir formation, dust thick as snowfall, name cards for every vanished child. The song hums through the walls. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: horror transfigured into witness; her documentation finally has a subject.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Bargain
chapters.summary: The founding families offer Paloma exemption if she surrenders her notebook and Dee's name; they frame it as mercy. She pretends to consider, buying time while Vesper teaches her the third verse letter by letter through the glass. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: temptation and contempt intertwined.

chapters.title: Dusk, Sung Backwards
chapters.summary: At dusk the town gathers to sing the collection-song over Dee. Paloma interrupts, reciting the third verse aloud—an indictment naming every taken child—while refusing to join the melody. The covenant inverts; the founders hear their own names in the lag. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: climactic defiance, terror held in check by purpose.

chapters.title: Roll Call
chapters.summary: The mirrors fall silent and true; the sub-basement empties as names return to records and memory. Vesper's portrait fades to blank canvas, released. Paloma's own reflection never comes back, but Dee reads the recovered roll call aloud, every name answered by 'here.' POV: Dee. Emotional beat: mourning braided with hard-won justice and quiet continuation.
